source.title: Noise-Driven Escape from Metastable Phases explains Grokking in Deep Neural Networks

record.file_problem: none; the full paper text, including appendices, is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study tests delayed, grokking-like generalization in a different setting and with a different method from the original algorithmic-dataset studies: deep linear networks on synthetic Gaussian data with L2-induced metastable trapping.
record.gate_note: The paper reports its own delayed-convergence and train/test-error results. The phase-diagram and barrier calculations are not separate grokking-behaviour results. Values reported from cited work are not included. The figure caption gives β = 0.03 for Fig. 1(a), while the main text and Appendix A state β = 0.32; rows below use the explicit main-text and appendix descriptions.
record.test_reason: The study reports its own grokking-like delays on non-algorithmic synthetic Gaussian data in deep linear networks. Each delay is turned on or off by the initialization protocol: fresh random weights versus checkpoints prepared in lower-rank metastable phases. This bears on V3's claim that the training regime, not algorithmic data, sets the delay. The traps are prepared deliberately, but initialization is the kind of regime lever V3 itself names, so the study counts as a test rather than induced behaviour.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors propose noise-activated escape from L2-created metastable phases as a candidate mechanism for grokking. They report Arrhenius scaling with Teff ∝ ηlr/B and reproduce a delayed train/test-gap closure under sparse sampling without memorization. They also claim the mechanism likely extends to nonlinear networks, but cite only prior and preliminary work for this, not experiments in this paper.
record.recipe_differences: The experiments use depth-3 linear networks, Gaussian data, L2 regularization, and deliberately selected metastable initializations, rather than small algorithmic datasets and their training/test accuracy curves.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported delay depends strongly on initialization protocol and metastable phase; the sparse-sampling result uses 25 training samples and β = 0.0025. Escape times vary with learning rate in the Arrhenius sweep.

fits_no_version.finding: Escape time from the rank-1 trap follows Arrhenius scaling in B/ηlr (R² = 0.991, ΔEeff = 0.15 ± 0.05).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The length of a grokking-like delay is set by SGD noise temperature (ηlr/B) through activated escape over a loss barrier.

record.peer_reviewed: HiLD 2026: 4th Workshop on High-dimensional Learning Dynamics
record.problems: The experiments are limited to deep linear networks and synthetic Gaussian tasks. The paper does not test algorithmic datasets or the claimed dependence of delay on training-set size across a sweep. The dense-data trapping results report delayed convergence without the canonical train/test dissociation; that dissociation is shown only in the separate sparse-sampling setup. Fig. 1(a)'s caption states β = 0.03, inconsistent with the main text and Appendix A, which state β = 0.32.

untested.parts: Images, text and molecules; sweeps of initialization scale or weight norm; any lazy-to-rich transition. The study also never shows a delay arising from standard random initialization; delays need prepared trapped checkpoints.
Not tested: no algorithmic datasets, accuracy measures or training-set-size sweep.
Not tested: no circuit formation or progress measures. The authors argue memorization is unnecessary, but only in a linear model that cannot memorize.
Not tested: no LLMs and no realistic data.
Not tested: no efficiency comparison, critical dataset size or ungrokking. L2 is used to build traps, not to favour a more efficient circuit.
Not tested: SGD only, with no adaptive optimizer and no floating-point controls.

missing.what: The spread of escape times across the 50 seeds for the Fig. 1(a) trapping runs; only single approximate τ values are given.

record.verdict_notes: Tranche changed from T2 to T3: it is a new setting, linear networks on Gaussian data. The Fig. 1(a) caption gives β = 0.03, while the text and Appendix A give 0.32. Appendix A says trapping checkpoints are first trained at βinit = 0, which conflicts with the stated βinit = 0.361 and 0.43. All rows use a single tiny model with D = 170 parameters.

versions.untested_parts: The study uses synthetic Gaussian data, not small algorithmic datasets, and does not test perfect training accuracy at chance test accuracy or whether delay grows as the training set shrinks.
It does not track formation of a generalizing circuit, removal of memorizing components, Fourier algorithms, or continuous progress measures anticipating a jump.
The study tests a synthetic Gaussian setting and initialization-dependent trapping, not images, text, molecules, initialization-scale sweeps, weight-norm sweeps, or a lazy-to-rich transition.
No LLM pretraining or fine-tuning on realistic data is studied.
The study does not test whether low norm favours a more efficient generalizing circuit, a critical dataset size, or ungrokking below such a size.
It does not compare identifiable algorithms learned across runs.
It does not test adaptive-optimizer instabilities or floating-point softmax limits.

rows.subject: deep linear network
rows.size_stated: L = 3, hidden width w = 10, D = 170 parameters
rows.operation_detail: Train from fresh random weights at β = 0.32; compare convergence time with trapped initializations.

conditions.value: fresh random weights drawn from N(0, 1/√w)
Gaussian data with d = 2 non-zero singular values

rows.value: τ ≈ 10 epochs; the model converges rapidly to the rank-2 global minimum.
rows.note: The paper presents this as the no-trapping comparison for the checkpoint-initialized conditions.
rows.check: Correct as the no-trap control: no delay arises from fresh random initialization. Its role is the comparison condition for R2 and R3.

rows.subject: deep linear network
rows.size_stated: L = 3, hidden width w = 10, D = 170 parameters
rows.operation_detail: Continue training at β = 0.32 from a checkpoint placed in the metastable rank-1 phase.

conditions.value: checkpoint trained to convergence at βinit = 0.361 > βc(1) = 0.360
Gaussian data with d = 2 non-zero singular values

rows.measure: Time in the rank-1 state before escape to rank-2
rows.value: τ ≈ 5500 epochs before abrupt escape to rank-2.
rows.note: The paper describes this as grokking-like delayed convergence caused by trapping.
rows.check: Delay is real (≈5500 vs ≈10 epochs). But the authors state the dense-data runs show no train/test gap; training error converges monotonically. This is a delayed convergence, not generalization delayed after training saturates. Only one representative value is given, although 50 seeds were run.

rows.measure: Time through rank-0 escape and subsequent rank-1 trapping
rows.value: Escapes to rank-1 after τ > 7000 epochs, then remains trapped there for an extended period; total delay τ > 10,000 epochs.
rows.note: The paper describes sequential trapping as producing staged delays.
rows.check: Same caveat as R2: a staged delay of over 10,000 epochs, but no train/test dissociation in the dense-data setting. The Fig. 1(a) caption gives β = 0.03, while the text and Appendix A give 0.32.

rows.subject: deep linear network
rows.size_stated: L = 3, hidden width w = 10, D = 170 parameters
rows.operation_detail: Train from a rank-1 trapped state on a sparse training subset.
rows.measure: Train and test MSE over training; escape from the rank-1 state
rows.value: Train MSE plateaus below test MSE; after ≈1500 epochs the model escapes to rank-2 and test error falls sharply, approaching train error within a small residual gap.
rows.note: The paper says training error cannot reach zero in this stochastic linear task; the final errors remain bounded by irreducible task noise.
rows.check: A train/test gap closes abruptly after ≈1500 epochs. But train MSE does not saturate first: the Discussion says both errors fall abruptly at escape. Errors are MSE, not accuracy, and a residual gap remains. The delay exists only because the model starts in a prepared rank-1 trap; the rank-1 checkpoint protocol at β = 0.0025 is not separately described.

rows.subject: deep linear network
rows.size_stated: L = 3, hidden width w = 10, D = 170 parameters
rows.operation_detail: Measure escape times from a rank-1 trapped state while varying the learning rate.
rows.measure: Arrhenius relationship between ln τ and 1/Teff
rows.value: Linear fit R2 = 0.991; extracted effective barrier ∆Eeff = 0.15 ± 0.05.
rows.note: This measures the noise-activated escape account and learning-rate dependence, not initialization scale or weight norm as named in V3.

relationships.condition: Deep linear network on synthetic Gaussian data; trapped checkpoint initialization versus fresh random initialization
relationships.reason: The delay is switched on by trapped initialization (≈5500 epochs, and over 10,000 for the rank-0 trap) and off by random initialization (≈10 epochs) on non-algorithmic data (R1, R2, R3).
relationships.display_finding: Trapped initialization delayed optimization to about 5,500 epochs or beyond 10,000 for the rank-0 trap, versus about 10 for random initialization, without canonical training–test separation.

source_check.label: supports
source_check.condition: Deep linear network on synthetic Gaussian data; trapped checkpoint initialization versus fresh random initialization
source_check.reason: R1–R3 establish initialization-dependent optimization delays, but Section 4.2 explicitly reports no canonical train/test dissociation in these dense-data runs. Checkpoint preparation also does not establish V3's initialization-scale or weight-norm switch. These results demonstrate only an incomplete analogue of the claimed effect.

relationships.condition: Dense data (512 samples) versus sparse sub-sampling (25 samples)
relationships.reason: Dense-data delays show no train/test dissociation. Under sparse sampling the gap closes, but train error also drops at escape rather than having saturated first (R2, R3, R4).
relationships.display_finding: With 512 samples, delays lacked training/test dissociation; with 25 samples, the gap closed as training error also fell at escape.

source_check.condition: Dense data (512 samples) versus sparse sub-sampling (25 samples)
source_check.reason: R2–R3 have delayed convergence without canonical train/test dissociation. R4 shows delayed gap closure, but both errors fall at escape rather than generalization improving after training error reaches its final level (Section 4.2).

relationships.reason: The delay appears only from checkpoints deliberately placed in metastable phases, not from initialization-scale or weight-norm settings of ordinary training. Fresh random initialization gives no delay (R1).
relationships.display_finding: Delays appeared from checkpoints deliberately placed in metastable phases, while fresh random initialization produced no delay.

source_check.label: limits_scope
source_check.reason: R1–R2 demonstrate a checkpoint-protocol effect, but no initialization-scale or weight-norm comparison is performed. The absence of that comparison is an untested part of V3, not evidence that its specified switch fails or requires qualification. The observed incomplete grokking signature is addressed by l0 and l1.
